    Distributed segmentation on SLURM¶

    run_distributed_segmentation spreads a whole slide over many Dask workers — CPU processes on one machine, or GPU jobs that SMINT submits to SLURM — and then stitches the tiles back together, so cells on tile boundaries come out whole and every nucleus belongs to exactly one cell.

    In this tutorial you will:

    1. run it with backend="local" (two CPU workers) on the synthetic image from Segment a whole slide;
    2. read the stitching log and the output tables;
    3. see the same call for SLURM GPU workers, with the numbers from a real run.

    Runtime: about a minute on 8 CPU cores. Requires: SMINT with the distributed extra (dask.distributed, dask-jobqueue, zarr, shapely) and Cellpose 3 for the built-in cyto3 / nuclei models.

    Download this notebook: 04_distributed_segmentation.ipynb

    How tiles are processed¶

    The image is cut into a grid of core tiles (chunk_size). Each worker segments its tile expanded by tile_overlap pixels on every side, so a cell on a boundary is seen whole by both neighbouring tiles. The worker writes only its core region into the shared label masks, but reports the outline of every object in the expanded tile. The coordinator then:

    1. stitches nuclei — duplicates from neighbouring tiles that overlap by more than stitch_merge_thresh (0.5) are merged; smaller overlaps are trimmed;
    2. drops cells that touch no nucleus, then stitches cells the same way;
    3. reconciles cells and nuclei so every nucleus sits in exactly one cell.

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.5, 5.5))
ax.imshow(image[1], cmap="gray")
for y in range(0, 1024, tile):

        ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x, y), tile, tile, fill=False, ec="#dd8a2e", lw=2))
x0, y0 = 512, 0   # the tile at top right, with its overlap margin
ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x0 - overlap, y0), tile + overlap, tile + overlap,
                       fill=False, ec="#d53f8c", lw=2, ls="--"))
ax.set_title("Core tiles (orange); one expanded tile (pink, dashed)")
ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])
plt.show()

    tile_overlap must be larger than the biggest cell's radius. Here cells are about 36 px across, so 64 px is plenty.

    1. Run on local workers¶

    Model parameters go in a dictionary per model, with the same keys as Cellpose: diameter, flow_threshold, cellprob_threshold and channels (Cellpose 3 convention, [main, nuclear], 1-based). use_gpu=False starts plain CPU workers; on a machine with GPUs and dask-cuda, use_gpu=True starts one worker per GPU.

    In [3]:
    Copied! 
    results = run_distributed_segmentation(
    image_path="data/synthetic_wsi.ome.tif",
    output_dir="distributed_seg",
    cell_model="cyto3",
    nuclei_model="nuclei",
    cell_params={"diameter": 36, "flow_threshold": 0.4,
                 "cellprob_threshold": 0.0, "channels": [2, 1]},
    nuclei_params={"diameter": 15, "flow_threshold": 0.4,
                   "cellprob_threshold": 0.0, "channels": [1, 0]},
    chunk_size=512, tile_overlap=64,
    backend="local", n_workers=2, use_gpu=False,
)
    results = run_distributed_segmentation( image_path="data/synthetic_wsi.ome.tif", output_dir="distributed_seg", cell_model="cyto3", nuclei_model="nuclei", cell_params={"diameter": 36, "flow_threshold": 0.4, "cellprob_threshold": 0.0, "channels": [2, 1]}, nuclei_params={"diameter": 15, "flow_threshold": 0.4, "cellprob_threshold": 0.0, "channels": [1, 0]}, chunk_size=512, tile_overlap=64, backend="local", n_workers=2, use_gpu=False, )

    Reading the log:

    • Tile k/4 (...): N cells, M nuclei — each tile counts every object in its expanded region, so cells near a boundary are counted by two tiles.
    • Stitched P polygons: A after merging, B after trim/remove — duplicates merged into one; overlapping leftovers trimmed or removed.
    • X of Y cell outlines touch no nucleus and were dropped.
    • Reconciled ... — the final cell and nucleus counts after every nucleus is assigned to one cell (a cell with no nucleus left is removed; a nucleus with no cell keeps its own outline as its cell).

    2. The outputs¶

    File Contents
    cells_outlines.csv, nuclei_outlines.csv One row per outline vertex: global_cell_id, x, y (IDs from 1, after stitching)
    cells_summary.csv One row per cell: global_cell_id, x_centroid, y_centroid, area, n_nuclei
    nuclei_summary.csv One row per nucleus, with cell_id: the global_cell_id of its cell
    cells.zarr, nuclei.zarr Full-resolution label masks, as written by the tiles (per-tile IDs, not the stitched ones)
    distributed_seg_<time>.log The log above

    On this image the stitched result has exactly as many cells as the truth table, each with one nucleus (n_nuclei above). The overlay shows the stitched outlines; compare the tile boundary with the split cells in Segment a whole slide.

    In [7]:
    Copied! 
    def composite(image, colours):
    rgb = np.zeros(image.shape[1:] + (3,))
    for channel, colour in zip(image, colours):
        lo, hi = np.percentile(channel, (1, 99.7))
        rgb += np.clip((channel - lo) / (hi - lo), 0, 1)[..., None] * np.asarray(colour)
    return np.clip(rgb, 0, 1)

cell_outlines = pd.read_csv(results["cells_csv_path"])
nuclei_outlines = pd.read_csv(results["nuclei_csv_path"])
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 6.5))
for ax in axes:
    ax.imshow(composite(image, [(0, 1, 1), (0, 0.8, 0)]))
    for outlines, colour in ((cell_outlines, "white"), (nuclei_outlines, "yellow")):
        for _, obj in outlines.groupby("global_cell_id"):
            ax.plot(obj.x, obj.y, color=colour, lw=0.8)
    ax.axvline(511.5, color="#dd8a2e", ls="--", lw=1.2); ax.axhline(511.5, color="#dd8a2e", ls="--", lw=1.2)
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])
axes[0].set_title("Stitched cells (white) and nuclei (yellow)")
axes[1].set(xlim=(412, 612), ylim=(300, 100), title="Across the x = 512 tile boundary")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

    3. On SLURM GPUs¶

    For a real slide, give each worker a GPU. With backend="slurm", SMINT starts the workers as SLURM jobs through dask-jobqueue; slurm takes dask_jobqueue.SLURMCluster options plus gpu_type, which adds --gres=gpu:<type>:1 to every worker job. The image and output_dir must be on storage every node can read.

    from smint.segmentation import run_distributed_segmentation

results = run_distributed_segmentation(
    image_path="sample3_tile_scan.ome.tif",           # OME-TIFF or OME-Zarr, on shared storage
    output_dir="sample3_segmentation",                # on shared storage too
    cell_model="/path/to/models/cpsam_finetuned",     # a fine-tuned Cellpose-SAM model
    nuclei_model="nuclei",
    cell_params={"diameter": 120, "flow_threshold": 0.6,
                 "cellprob_threshold": -2.5, "channels": [2, 1]},
    nuclei_params={"diameter": 25, "flow_threshold": 0.3,
                   "cellprob_threshold": 0.2, "channels": [1, 0]},
    chunk_size=1048, tile_overlap=256,
    backend="slurm", n_workers=4,
    slurm={"queue": "gpuq", "gpu_type": "A30", "memory": "64GB"},
)

    This is the call behind the measured run in the worked examples: a 4096 × 4096 px Sample 3 tile scan, 16 tiles, 4 A30 workers, Cellpose 4 with a fine-tuned model. It logged:

    Tiles: 16 of 1048 px, 256 px overlap
4 worker(s) ready
Stitched 66 polygons: 44 after merging, 44 after trim/remove
30 of 103 cell outlines touch no nucleus and were dropped
Stitched 73 polygons: 43 after merging, 43 after trim/remove
Reconciled 43 cells / 44 nuclei -> 44 cells / 44 nuclei
Done in 0.6 min

    Run the coordinator itself as a small CPU job: it only submits the GPU workers and stitches their results. For example, with the call above saved as segment.py:

    #!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --partition=regular
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=2
#SBATCH --mem=16G
#SBATCH --time=04:00:00
python segment.py
